The other half is capture quality: hologram glare, curved cards and poor lighting fail before decoding starts, so the useful engineering is in guiding the capture and failing with a message the user can act on.

modules.name: FAQPilot - Grounded RAG
modules.desc: Your cleanest RAG story, with the two things most RAG demos lack: citations and a real evaluation set.
modules.bullet: Built FAQPilot, a grounded RAG support assistant answering from cited excerpts of user guides and release notes, validated across 500+ Q&A sessions; projected to deflect 60% of support tickets and 100+ agent-hours daily.

concepts.one: The model may only answer from retrieved passages, and every claim points back at the passage that supports it. Grounding is the constraint; citation is the proof.
concepts.analogy: An open-book exam where you must write the page number next to every answer. It does not make you smarter - it makes you checkable.
points: **"I don't know" must be a first-class outcome.** If retrieval returns nothing relevant, the correct answer is a refusal plus a route to a human - not a fluent guess.
**Citations change user behaviour**, which is the real product win: a support agent who can click through to the source trusts and verifies rather than accepting blindly.
**Faithfulness vs relevance** are different failures. A faithful answer is supported by the retrieved text; a relevant answer addresses the question. You can fail either independently.
Force the model to emit a **passage ID per claim**, then verify the ID exists before rendering. A hallucinated citation is worse than none because it looks rigorous.
Release notes make **freshness** a first-class concern - the correct answer changes when the product changes, so stale chunks are actively wrong.

code.cap: Refuse-by-default, and verify every citation before rendering

qa.q: How do you stop it answering confidently when retrieval finds nothing?
a: Two gates. Before generation, a relevance floor on the retrieval score - if the top hit is below it, escalate without ever calling the model, because a model handed irrelevant passages will still write something.

After generation, an explicit refusal token the prompt requires when the passages are insufficient, plus citation verification: every cited passage ID must exist in what was actually retrieved. A fabricated citation is the tell that the model went off-book, and it fails closed to a human.

qa.q: How did you validate it across 500+ Q&A sessions?
a: A curated evaluation set of real support questions with reviewed reference answers, scored on the two dimensions separately: did retrieval surface the right passage, and was the generated answer faithful to it. Separating them matters because they fail for different reasons and need different fixes.

Retrieval quality I would score as recall@k against the known-correct passage, which is cheap and objective. Answer faithfulness needs human review on a sample, with an LLM-judge used to widen coverage - calibrated against the human labels rather than trusted on its own.

qa.q: You said 'projected to deflect 60%'. What does projected mean here?
a: It is modelled, not observed - the share of historical tickets whose answer existed in the documentation corpus, which is the ceiling on what deflection could reach. It is not a measured deflection rate in production.

The honest measured version would be: of sessions where FAQPilot answered, what fraction still resulted in a human ticket. I would want that number before defending 60% as an outcome rather than an upper bound.

concepts.trap: "Projected" appears twice on your résumé - here and on the $10M. Both are legitimate; both must be volunteered by you rather than discovered by the interviewer.

modules.name: Your Numbers & The Scale Gap
modules.desc: Ruthless section. Every number you print is a question you volunteered. And there is one category of number missing from your résumé that a Google interviewer will look for immediately.

concepts.t: The rule: every number is a question
concepts.one: You have printed roughly fifteen metrics. Assume each one gets "how did you measure that?" - and that a number you cannot defend costs more than the number gained.
concepts.analogy: Every claim on a CV is a door you built into your own house. Some of them you have not checked are locked.
points: For each number, know four things: **definition** (of what), **denominator**, **window**, **source** (which dashboard or query).
A number you cannot source should be **found or cut** - never estimated live. Estimating on the spot is the failure mode that ends loops.
**Volunteer the caveats.** Saying "that's projected, not booked" before being asked converts a vulnerability into a credibility signal.
Rehearse the three most attackable out loud: 67% fraud reduction, 95% note accuracy, $10M projected ARR.
Attribution matters as much as measurement: say what *you* built versus what the team or business did.
concepts.trap: Rounding up under pressure, or agreeing with an interviewer's inflated restatement. If they say "so you saved the company ten million" - correct it immediately.

concepts.t: The scale gap - go and get these numbers
concepts.one: Your résumé is rich in business metrics and empty of engineering scale. There is no QPS, no data volume, no concurrency, no p95 anywhere. For a Google L4 loop, that is the single highest-leverage gap you can close this month.
concepts.analogy: A chef's CV listing revenue and covers but never how many plates left the pass at peak. Peak throughput is the number the kitchen actually judges you on.
points: **Go and find:** requests per second at peak on the services you own, and the p50/p95 latency alongside it.
**Go and find:** concurrent users or sessions at peak, and the database size - row counts on your largest tables, total storage.
**Go and find:** the real before/after percentiles for the Copilot rebuild, and how many Copilot requests per day flow through the agentic runtime.
**Go and find:** e-KYC verifications per day at peak, and the ledger's write rate in the billing layer.

Where you genuinely cannot get a number, use a bounded, honest statement: "I don't have the exact QPS; the service backs 10,000+ practices and peaks during US clinic hours, roughly 9am–5pm across four time zones." That still demonstrates you think in load shapes.
This is the difference between "built a feature" and "operated a system", and it is exactly what an L4 interviewer is listening for.

qa.q: What scale does your service run at?
a: This is the question you must not fumble. Have peak QPS, p95 latency, and data volume memorised for at least one service you own.

The structure that works: load shape, then throughput, then latency, then data size. 'Traffic is diurnal and follows US clinic hours across four time zones, so peak is roughly Nx the trough. At peak we serve about X requests per second with p95 at Y milliseconds. The largest table is Z rows and the working set fits in cache.'

concepts.say: I don't have that number in front of me - let me give you what I do know and the shape of it. [Then give load shape, tenants, and what you do know.] I'd rather be precise than guess.

concepts.t: Rewriting a bullet with scale in it
concepts.one: Once you have the numbers, the strongest bullets carry both a business outcome and an engineering scale figure. Here is the shape.
concepts.analogy: A before-and-after photo needs a ruler in the frame. The outcome tells them it mattered; the scale tells them it was hard.
points: **Current:** "Cut Charm Copilot latency 8-15s to 2-5s..." - outcome, no scale.
**With scale:** "...across N Copilot requests/day at M peak QPS, taking p95 from Xs to Ys and TTFT under 1s."
The pattern is: **what changed** + **by how much** + **at what load** + **which percentile**.
Do not fabricate to fill the template. A bullet with a real outcome and no scale beats a bullet with an invented QPS every single time - and invented numbers collapse under one follow-up.
Apply the same treatment to e-KYC (verifications/day) and the billing ledger (writes/day).
concepts.trap: Do not invent or round these to make the template fit. The whole point of adding scale is credibility; a number you cannot source destroys the thing you were trying to buy.
